overview: The Solankis, also called the Chaulukyas of Gujarat, governed a major western Indian kingdom from Anahilapataka, modern Patan. This is a different dynasty from the Chalukyas of the Deccan. The imported 1100 to 1200 interval captures an influential century within a longer history. Its broad Gujarat, Rajasthan and eastward outline simplifies changing conquests and subordinate rulers; it is not a surveyed boundary held unchanged for a hundred years.

periods.title: Earlier kingdom and monumental building
periods.summary: Solanki rule and major eleventh-century water and temple projects predate this map interval.

periods.title: Jayasimha and expanding royal administration
periods.summary: Jayasimha’s era saw stronger document administration and the consolidation of royal power.

periods.title: Kumarapala’s influential court
periods.summary: Kumarapala patronized learning; Hemachandra connected grammar with royal history.

periods.title: Later twelfth-century rule
periods.summary: The dynasty continued after Kumarapala; 1200 is the imported map cutoff, not its fall.

periods.title: Later transition to Vaghela power
periods.summary: Vaghela leaders gained practical authority and established independent supremacy in the 1240s.

sections.title: A kingdom ran on records as well as armies

items.text: The kingdom’s reach could extend beyond Gujarat. Inscriptions associated with Kumarapala’s officers occur at Udayapura near Bhilsa in Malwa. Such records help historians trace political power beyond the capital, while reminding us that local officers and subordinate rulers mattered alongside the king.

Royal copper-plate grants became more standardized around the beginning of the twelfth century. Historian Masahiko Mita connects this change with the emergence of a document office in the late eleventh century. Keeping consistent records was one of the quieter achievements of government, with consequences for land and revenue.

In these royal grants, the king appeared as donor, announcer and issuer. Mita distinguishes this regular form from documents issued by subordinate rulers. A copper plate was therefore more than a durable receipt: its wording displayed who claimed the right to grant land.

Rani-ki-Vav at Patan was built in the eleventh century, before the displayed map interval, and is traditionally attributed to Queen Udayamati, wife of Bhima I. Its memorial purpose joined family remembrance to a substantial public water structure. Royal women could leave their mark on a city’s practical landscape.

The stepwell descends through seven levels of stairs and carved panels toward stored water. More than five hundred principal sculptures mix sacred and secular subjects. The builders made the descent itself an architectural experience: getting water could involve walking down into an extraordinary stone world.

UNESCO’s account links the well’s later silting to thirteenth-century flooding and changes to the Saraswati riverbed. Burial helped preserve much of its sculpture for centuries. The same environmental change that ended its original water function helped shelter evidence of the craftspeople who built it.

Another Patan water project, Sahastralinga Talav, renewed an earlier reservoir during Siddharaja Jayasimha’s reign. The district’s monument account notes that both rulers and citizens sponsored lakes, wells and reservoirs. Supplying water depended on repeated maintenance and patronage, not just one spectacular new building.

At Modhera, an eleventh-century Sun temple combines a shrine, an assembly hall and a stepped tank. Sculptors filled its surfaces with gods, musicians, birds and animals; ceiling scenes draw on the Ramayana and Mahabharata. Architecture provided space for gathering while its carvings carried stories and religious imagery.

sections.title: Food cargoes, family gifts and a port’s income

items.text: A Mangrol inscription from the mid-1140s records a temple named for Sahajiga, father of the donors Somaraja and Muluka. Muluka assigned revenue to support its worship. This family memorial connected kinship, local leadership and the continuing costs of maintaining a religious institution.

The same record lists dues on grain carts, bullock and donkey loads, camels carrying betel leaves, and salt production. These are useful glimpses of working lives: growers, carters, pack-animal handlers and sellers kept goods moving. A temple’s accounts can unexpectedly turn into a map of everyday trade.

Leading people at Choravad also dedicated a tree-lined well near a village road, with royal permission. The inscription describes an existing, bounded property. Water facilities could be shared civic assets whose support and ownership were carefully recorded, rather than merely holes somebody dug and forgot.

Cambay’s maritime importance depended on its inland connections. Research links the rise of Chaulukya power with routes joining the coast, agricultural districts and intermediary markets. A twelfth-century Jewish business letter also records a voyage through Diu toward Aden. Gujarat’s economy connected inland growers with people travelling far across the sea.

sections.title: Learning, unequal households and surviving words

items.text: Hemachandra composed a work in 1160 that illustrated grammar through praised deeds of royal patrons, including Kumarapala. Language lessons could also tell readers how a ruler wished to be remembered. This was learned courtly literature; its survival does not tell us that every child attended school.

A surviving copy made in 1428 shows Hemachandra teaching Kumarapala. The monk carries a cloth to avoid swallowing insects and a broom to protect small creatures in his path. This later illustration preserves a Jain ideal of avoiding harm, while remaining a later artistic portrayal rather than an eyewitness portrait.

The Lekhapaddhati preserves actual and model documents used by scribes, including credit agreements, mortgages and private letters. Its materials span several centuries of Gujarat’s history. Forms for everyday obligations show why trained writers mattered: making a promise about property or money could require specialized language.

Some documents in that collection concern enslaved girls and reveal the power their owners exercised over their work and treatment. Courtly learning and magnificent temples existed alongside deep household inequalities. These records help recover people whose choices were sharply restricted and whose own voices rarely survive.

नमः शिवाय, namaḥ śivāya, means “Salutation to Shiva.” This Sanskrit phrase opens the Mangrol stone record dated Vikrama Samvat 1202, in the mid-1140s. It appears here in modern Devanagari type, following the published transcription of the inscription, rather than reproducing the stone’s individual carved letters.

ending.text: The 1200 map cutoff does not mark the dynasty’s end. During the thirteenth century, Vaghela leaders accumulated authority, and Visaladeva established independent supremacy in the 1240s. This was a transfer of ruling power within a continuing regional society. Gujarat’s water monuments, trade and learned traditions outlived the Solanki court.
